name: Kechimyaku Zakura (The Blood-Lineage Cherry)
species: Matsumae Hayazaki Cherry (Prunus sp., cultivar 'Matsumae-hayazaki', presumed Prunus lannesiana x Prunus verecunda hybrid)

location.address: Kozenji Temple, Matsushiro, Matsumae, Matsumae District, Hokkaido (address block 松城303)

access: Free, temple grounds open to the public. JR Kikonai station, then Hakodate Bus approx. 1.5 hours to Matsushiro-shimo stop, then 10 minute walk.
transport: Matsushiro-shimo bus stop (Hakodate Bus from JR Kikonai) + 10 min walk

best_time.label: late April into early May, when the blossom opens

story:
Matsumae grows more than 250 cherry cultivars and one of them began here. This is the mother tree of the Matsumae-hayazaki, also known as Naden, thought to be a cross between Takasago and Kasumizakura; every tree of that cultivar traces back to this one.

It stands in the grounds of Kozenji, a temple founded in 1575 in what became the northernmost castle town in Japan. The cultivar is believed to have reached Hokkaido through the Kitamae-bune trade, the coastal shipping route that carried goods and plants north along the Sea of Japan.

Its age depends on who you read. Japanese Wikipedia gives over 200 years in one place and over 280 in another. Garden and tourism sources say over 300. None of them names a method, so the honest span runs from a little over two hundred years to a little over three hundred. The measurements are not in dispute: eight metres tall, five and a half metres around.

Hokkaido designated it a Memorial Tree in 1973. The name comes from a story the temple still tells, about a maiden and a blood lineage, and it is the reason people know this cherry by name rather than as one more tree in a famous blossom town. It is still listed as a bloom-forecast site on the national cherry tracker, which is a plain way of saying it flowered again this spring. Free, on open temple ground, ten minutes on foot from the Matsushiro-shimo bus stop.

name: The Great Mulberry of Usune
age_estimate: traditionally said to be roughly 1,500 years; a 1991 official survey estimated 300+ years

location.address: 2083 Machida-cho, Numata City, Gunma Prefecture (Ishizumi-cho area, formerly Usune Village, Tone District)

access: Free, viewable at any time; a maintained wooden viewing walkway (recently repaired) leads to the tree, on cultivated land near Ishizumi Daijingu shrine. Parking available in spare space at the shrine. Visitors asked to avoid times that would inconvenience nearby residents. Caution advised on the walkway in wet or snowy weather.
transport: Bus from JR Numata Station (Joetsu Line), Kan-etsu Kotsu Sayama Line, alight at 'Ishizumi Ippommatsu' stop, 2 min walk. Or 15 min drive from Numata IC on the Kan-etsu Expressway.
story:
Japan made this tree a National Natural Monument in 1956, which is a strange honour for a mulberry. In Gunma a mulberry is a leaf crop, grown low and picked bare to feed silkworms. This one was left alone: Numata City measures it at 13.65 metres tall and 5.67 metres around, and it is widely reported as the largest wild mulberry in the country.

It stands on farmland in what was Usune village, inside the Gunma silk story that runs through the Tomioka Silk Mill, now a World Heritage site. Farmers here treated it as a guardian of silkworm rearing, and when frost stripped the mulberry crop on surrounding farms, its leaves fed the worms. By local tradition it also served as a benchmark in a Maebashi domain land survey in 1686.

Its age is a dispute nobody has settled. The city repeats the traditional figure of roughly 1,500 years; a 1991 official survey suggested something nearer 300. The Cultural Affairs Agency's own record disagrees on the dimensions too, listing 10.7 metres tall and five metres round at chest height. In 2018 the tree was under treatment for pest damage.

Viewing is free and at any hour, along a maintained wooden walkway to the trunk, with parking at Ishizumi Daijingu shrine next door. The walkway is slippery in wet or snowy weather.
